texts: mixed: the lighting, the East Row lanterns, sundown and the date all land, but two things go wrong. The parse adds a per-keeper rule that derives that EACH keeper lit the whole East Row, which the sentence does not say, and the verb "lit" lands on the same symbol that "mist-light" inherits two sentences later, so anything asking about light conflates the lighting with the substance. Write: "Together, the keepers kindled the lanterns of the East Row at sundown on day 3 of Year 1." — "together" makes it one joint act, the lowercase "keepers" stops it being read as a name, and "kindled" keeps the event off the light symbol.
good. the burning parses with the lanterns as the burners and mire-essence as the fuel consumed, and the per-lantern rule it adds is harmless here — each lantern did burn essence.

mixed: the producing itself is right, but the per-lantern rule hands the one mist-light referent to every lantern, so the parse derives that each lantern separately produced that same light. Write: "Together, the lanterns produced mist-light."
good. the mist-light attracts a swarm of nightmoths, with the moths correctly recorded as unchanged by the attracting.

mixed: this mints a SECOND, unrelated swarm — nothing links these moths to the ones the mist-light just attracted, so the chain lanterns → mist-light → moths → threads breaks here. Make them the same moths: "Many of the nightmoths gathered at the lanterns of the East Row."
good. the landing is recorded both for the swarm as a whole and for each moth, with the lanterns as the place.

bad: "left silken threads" is parsed as if the leaving changed or created the threads, where every other sentence treats these same threads as merely moved or handled — and the per-moth rule repeats that error once per moth, so a question about the threads being deposited will not match. Write: "The nightmoths deposited silken threads on the lanterns."

mixed: the collecting itself is complete (Pell, the threads, the lanterns as source, dawn, day 4 of Year 1), but nothing orders it after the day-3 lighting — with no month stated, "day 4" and "day 3" are bare day numbers the engine cannot compare, so the episode's chronology is not derivable. Write: "On the next day, day 4 of Year 1, Pell collected the silken threads from the lanterns at dawn." — the "next day" wording is what makes the translator emit the explicit ordering.
good. Pell, the threads and Cauldron Hall as the destination all land, with Cauldron Hall recorded as a named hall.

bad: "the second cauldron" has no licensed form — the translator can only record a rank against a stated ordering, and none is stated here, so the rule-conforming output drops "second" and the parse no longer says which of the three cauldrons was used. Give the cauldron an identity instead of a rank: "Hesper boiled the silken threads in sea-water in Cauldron Two on day 4 of Year 1."

good. the mire-essence gets its own referent, the cauldron is its place, and "by evening" is carried as a deadline; it reuses the boiling sentence's cauldron, so it will follow whatever label that sentence ends up using.
good. the storing parses with Hesper, the mire-essence and two clay vessels, with both the count and the material kept.

mixed: the same two problems as the opening sentence — the per-keeper rule derives that each keeper lit the whole East Row, and this "Keepers" mints a second keeper group with nothing tying it to the day-3 keepers. The stored mire-essence is correctly carried as the means and does point back at the essence stored in the previous sentence. Write: "Together, the keepers kindled the lanterns of the East Row with the stored mire-essence at sundown on day 4 of Year 1."
